title: Ch-T-A
hook: chet, sin, means missing the mark, as slingers "not missing" (Judges 20:16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Y-R-H: yarah, to shoot, to point, Jonathan's arrows and Judah showing the way. Your line was torah means aiming. Did you take your first step toward the target? Today, what happens when the arrow goes wide. Day one thousand three hundred ninety.

Last seconds of a high-school game. A kid steps to the free-throw line, bounces the ball, breathes, shoots. It clangs off the front of the rim. The gym goes quiet. Nobody in the bleachers calls it evil. Nobody says the kid is a bad person. It's a miss. The coach will say: bend your knees, follow through, again. Hold onto that gym, because a Hebrew word for sin comes from a verb the Bible uses for exactly this. Chet, tet, alef: Ch-T-A. To miss.
screen: `OFF THE FRONT OF THE RIM.` → `NOBODY CALLS IT EVIL.` → `CH-T-A: TO MISS.`

segments.voice: Turn Ch-T-A four ways. First, the slingers. The book of Judges describes a company of left-handed fighters from the tribe of Benjamin who could sling a stone at a hair and not miss. Not miss, in Hebrew, is lo yachati, from this very root. Before it's a moral word, it's a word for a stone that flies wide. Second, the noun. Chet is one of the Bible's words for sin, and you can hear the slingers inside it. In this picture, sin is an aim that went off: a target that was there, a stone that didn't reach it. Third, nobody is perfect. Ecclesiastes says it flatly: "For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not." Even the good miss. The verse doesn't say the target is fake, or that aim doesn't matter. It says that everyone who shoots will sometimes miss. Fourth, why we miss. Proverbs adds a detail anyone who's been late can recognize: the one who hurries with his feet misses, again from Ch-T-A. Speed, carelessness, a stone thrown without looking. Put it together with yesterday. If Torah is aiming, chet is the miss, and the two belong to the same practice. A miss is serious. Someone can get hurt by a stone that goes wide. But a miss can also be studied. Where did it go? Was I rushing? What would I adjust? The coach at the free-throw line is already asking the question this root asks.
screen: `SLINGERS WHO DID NOT MISS.` · `CHET: A STONE THAT FLIES WIDE.` · `NOT A RIGHTEOUS MAN WHO SINNETH NOT.` · `HURRYING FEET MISS.` · then, large: `חֵטְא`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: aim better once. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small miss from the past few days. A sharp word, a promise that slipped, a moment you rushed past someone. Don't argue with it and don't punish yourself. Just look at where the stone landed. Then ask the coach's questions. Was I hurrying? What was I actually aiming at? What one adjustment would bring the next shot closer? Find the adjustment, and hold it. If you pray, you can bring the miss into the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Ch-T-A. Chet, tet, alef: the root of chet, sin, from a verb for missing the mark, like a slinger's stone that goes wide. Today's word.
Your line: sin is missing the mark. Today, the next time you're about to repeat that miss, slow your feet down, and take the shot with the adjustment. Day one thousand three hundred ninety.

howItsDone: In the Yom Kippur liturgy Jews recite the Al Chet, a confession whose lines begin "for the sin," al chet, said together as a community.

original.note: Hebrew: sin; from the root Ch-T-A, to miss the mark.

trapdoor: what you thought: sin means being a bad person.
what it means: chet, the Hebrew word for sin, comes from a verb for missing a target.
what a scholar hears: Judges 20:16 uses the root for slingers who did not miss, and Proverbs 19:2 for hurrying feet.

notes: Editor: 'Hebrew's everyday word for sin' (an unsourced frequency claim) softened to 'a Hebrew word for sin'.
Judges 20:16 paraphrased (left-handed men of Benjamin who slung at a hair and did not miss, lo yachati); the verse's number of men is omitted on purpose. Confirm.
Proverbs 19:2 paraphrased: 'he that hasteth with his feet sinneth' (chote). Confirm the reading as 'misses'.
'Chet is one of the Bible's words for sin' (alongside avon and pesha); confirm.
Root spelled Ch-T-A per the index; the Hebrew letters are chet, tet, alef. The word segment names them in that order.
